items.title: The Beta density has finite positive Lebesgue integral
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. For every $\alpha,\beta>0$, the nonnegative function
$p\mapsto p^{\alpha-1}(1-p)^{\beta-1}$ is Lebesgue measurable on $(0,1)$ and
$$\int_{(0,1)}p^{\alpha-1}(1-p)^{\beta-1}\,d\lambda_1(p)
=B(\alpha,\beta)=\frac{\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)}{\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)}
\in(0,\infty).$$
items.strategy: Use compact interior truncations, the bounded Riemann-to-Lebesgue result, monotone convergence, and the Beta-Gamma identity.

references.title: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §2.1
Johnson, Ott & Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, Chapter 3, §3.1

items.title: The Binomial count has its usual probability mass function
items.statement:
If $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are independent Bernoulli$(p)$ variables with $0<p<1$ and
$n\in\mathbb N_0$, then their sum $S_n$ has
$$\mathbb P(S_n=y)=\binom ny p^y(1-p)^{n-y},\qquad y=0,\ldots,n.$$
For $n=0$, the empty sum is zero and the sole mass is one.
items.strategy: Partition by the success-index subset and sum the independent Bernoulli probabilities, including n=0.

references.title: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §2.1
Johnson, Ott & Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, Chapter 3, §3.1

items.title: The shape-rate Gamma density is normalized
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. For $a,b>0$,
$$\int_{(0,\infty)}\frac{b^a}{\Gamma(a)}x^{a-1}e^{-bx}\,d\lambda_1(x)=1.$$
items.strategy: Scale the Euler Gamma integral by t=bx under Countable Choice and normalize the shape-rate kernel.

references.title: Johnson, Ott & Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, Chapter 5, §§5.2.1–5.2.2
Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §§2.1, 2.4

items.title: Exposure-parameterized Poisson law
items.statement:
For exposure $e\ge0$ and rate $\lambda>0$, define
$Y\sim\operatorname{Pois}(e\lambda)$ to have the scalar Poisson count law with
parameter $e\lambda$. Thus for $e>0$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=y\mid\lambda,e)=e^{-e\lambda}\frac{(e\lambda)^y}{y!},
\qquad y\in\mathbb N_0,$$
with $0^0=1$; when $e=0$ this is the point mass at $y=0$. The law is normalized
by [[lem-poisson-count-law-normalization-and-moments]]. A zero-exposure
positive count has likelihood zero.
items.strategy: Reparameterize the scalar Poisson law by exposure times rate; preserve the zero-exposure point mass.

references.title: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §2.4
Günter Last and Mathew Penrose, Lectures on the Poisson Process, 2017, Chapter 1

items.title: Conjugate-form prior for an exponential family
items.statement:
Let $\eta:\Theta\to\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^k$ be measurable, let
$\rho$ be a sigma-finite measure on the parameter space, and let $A$ be the
log-partition function in [[def-exponential-family]]. For
$\chi\in\mathbb R^k$ and $\kappa\in\mathbb R$, define
$$Z(\chi,\kappa)=\int_\Theta
\exp\{\eta(\theta)^T\chi-\kappa A(\eta(\theta))\}\,\rho(d\theta).$$
When $0<Z(\chi,\kappa)<\infty$, the **conjugate-form prior**
$\Pi_{\chi,\kappa}$ is the probability measure with density
$$\frac{\exp\{\eta(\theta)^T\chi-\kappa A(\eta(\theta))\}}
{Z(\chi,\kappa)}$$
relative to $\rho$. If this finite-positive condition fails, this notation
does not designate a probability prior.
items.strategy: Define the conjugate-form prior only when its parameter-measure normalizer is finite and positive.

references.title: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §2.4
Charles J. Geyer, Stat 5421 Lecture Notes: Exponential Families, 2020

items.title: Finite-dimensional Euclidean space with its Borel sigma-algebra is standard Borel
items.statement: For every natural $n\ge1$, let $\mathbb R^n$ be the set of functions $x:n\to\mathbb R$ with its finite-product topology and Borel sigma-algebra ([[def-product-topology]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Then $(\mathbb R^n,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n))$ is standard Borel.
items.strategy: Compare the maximum metric topology with the product topology, then use completeness and rational density.

references.title: O. Biskup, MATH 275D notes, Chapter 2: Kolmogorov Extension Theorem

items.title: Dirichlet simplex density kernel
items.statement:
For $k\ge2$ and positive coordinates $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_k$, write
$\Delta_{k-1}=\{(p_1,\ldots,p_{k-1})\in(0,\infty)^{k-1}:
\sum_{j<k}p_j<1\}$ and set $p_k=1-\sum_{j<k}p_j$. The **Dirichlet density
kernel** is the nonnegative function
$$q_\alpha(p_1,\ldots,p_{k-1})
=\frac{\Gamma(\alpha_+)}{\prod_{j=1}^k\Gamma(\alpha_j)}
\prod_{j=1}^kp_j^{\alpha_j-1},\qquad
\alpha_+=\sum_{j=1}^k\alpha_j,$$
relative to coordinate Lebesgue measure $dp_1\cdots dp_{k-1}$. This item
defines the density function; [[thm-dirichlet-density-normalization]] proves
that it integrates to one.
items.strategy: Define the nonnegative coordinate-simplex density kernel with Gamma factors and declare its reference measure.

references.title: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §3.4
Gero Walter, A Technical Note on the Dirichlet-Multinomial Model, 2013

items.title: The Multinomial mass function is normalized
items.statement:
For $k\ge1$, $n\in\mathbb N_0$, and $p_j\ge0$ with $\sum_jp_j=1$, the masses
$$\frac{n!}{\prod_{j=1}^ky_j!}\prod_{j=1}^kp_j^{y_j},
\qquad y_j\in\mathbb N_0,\quad\sum_jy_j=n,$$
sum to one, using $0^0=1$.
items.strategy: Apply the finite multinomial theorem to the probability vector, checking n=0 and zero coordinates.

references.title: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §3.4
Gero Walter, A Technical Note on the Dirichlet-Multinomial Model, 2013

items.title: Conditional law of a jointly Gaussian block with positive-definite observed covariance
items.statement:
Assume AC. Let $X\in\mathbb R^d$ and $Y\in\mathbb R^m$, with $d,m\ge1$, be
jointly multivariate normal with mean $(a,b)$ and positive-semidefinite block
covariance
$$\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}A&C\\C^T&B\end{pmatrix},$$
where $B$ is positive definite. Then
$$S=A-CB^{-1}C^T$$
is positive semidefinite, and for every $y\in\mathbb R^m$ the probability law
$$K(y,\cdot)=N_d\!\left(a+CB^{-1}(y-b),S\right)$$
is defined. The map $K$ is a probability kernel and is a conditional law of
$X$ given $Y$: for all Borel $E\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ and
$F\subseteq\mathbb R^m$,
$$\mathbb P(X\in E,Y\in F)=\int_F K(y,E)\,\mathbb P_Y(dy).$$
The covariance $A$ and the conditional covariance $S$ may be singular.
Positive definiteness of $B$ is required; no pseudoinverse formula for
singular $B$ is asserted.
items.strategy: Prove the Schur complement is PSD, subtract the regression residual, use Gaussian block independence, and verify the conditional-kernel identity.

references.title: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §3.5
Simo Särkkä, Bayesian Filtering and Smoothing, Appendix A.1

items.title: The sum of exponential-family statistics is sufficient for an IID sample
items.statement:
Assume AC. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be standard Borel, let $\mu$ be a
sigma-finite measure, and let $(P_\eta)_{\eta\in\Omega}$ be a nonempty
exponential family of [[def-exponential-family]] with density
$p_\eta(y)=h(y)\exp\{\eta^TT(y)-A(\eta)\}$. For each finite $n\ge1$, the IID
sample law $P_\eta^{\otimes n}$ has density
$$\prod_{i=1}^nh(y_i)\exp\!\left\{\eta^T\sum_{i=1}^nT(y_i)-nA(\eta)\right\}$$
relative to $\mu^{\otimes n}$, and
$T_n(y_1,\ldots,y_n)=\sum_{i=1}^nT(y_i)$ is sufficient for the sample.
No full-rank, completeness, or converse characterization is asserted.
items.strategy: Construct the IID product density, factor its likelihood ratio through the sum statistic, and apply the standard-Borel common-reference criterion under AC.

references.title: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §2.4
Peter Kempthorne, MIT 18.655 Lecture Note 6: Sufficiency

items.title: Beta distribution
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. For $\alpha,\beta>0$, the **Beta distribution** $\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)$ is the probability measure on $(0,1)$ with density
$$f_{\alpha,\beta}(p)=\frac{p^{\alpha-1}(1-p)^{\beta-1}}{B(\alpha,\beta)}$$
relative to Lebesgue measure. The finite positive normalization follows from
[[lem-beta-density-normalization]]. The open interval is the parameter domain;
no endpoint atoms are included.
items.strategy: Define the Beta law using the proved finite-positive Beta kernel normalizer; state the open-interval convention.

references.title: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §2.1
Johnson, Ott & Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, Chapter 3, §3.1

items.title: Shape-rate Gamma distribution
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. For shape $a>0$ and rate $b>0$, the **shape-rate Gamma distribution**
$\operatorname{Gamma}(a,b)$ is the probability measure on $(0,\infty)$ with
density
$$f_{a,b}(\lambda)=\frac{b^a}{\Gamma(a)}\lambda^{a-1}e^{-b\lambda}$$
relative to Lebesgue measure. Its normalization is proved in
[[lem-gamma-density-normalization]]. The second argument is a rate, not a scale.
items.strategy: Define Gamma in shape-rate convention using the proved positive finite Gamma density integral.

references.title: Johnson, Ott & Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, Chapter 5, §§5.2.1–5.2.2
Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §2.4

items.title: Dirichlet density normalization by iterated Beta integrals
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. For $k\ge2$ and $\alpha_j>0$,
$$\int_{\Delta_{k-1}}\prod_{j=1}^kp_j^{\alpha_j-1}\,dp_1\cdots dp_{k-1}
=\frac{\prod_{j=1}^k\Gamma(\alpha_j)}{\Gamma(\alpha_+)}\in(0,\infty).$$
Consequently the density kernel in [[def-dirichlet-density-kernel]] has
integral one.
items.strategy: Use the stick-breaking diffeomorphism, compute its Jacobian, factor into Beta integrals, and cancel Gamma factors.

references.title: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §3.4
Gero Walter, A Technical Note on the Dirichlet-Multinomial Model, 2013

items.title: Multinomial distribution
items.statement:
For $k\ge1$, $n\in\mathbb N_0$, and $p=(p_1,\ldots,p_k)$ with $p_j\ge0$ and
$\sum_jp_j=1$, the **Multinomial distribution**
$\operatorname{Multinomial}(n,p)$ is the law on count vectors
$y\in\mathbb N_0^k$ with $\sum_jy_j=n$ and masses
$$\mathbb P(Y=y)=\frac{n!}{\prod_jy_j!}\prod_jp_j^{y_j},$$
using $0^0=1$. The masses sum to one by
[[lem-multinomial-law-normalization]]. For $k=1$ or $n=0$, this law is
degenerate at its unique admissible count vector.
items.strategy: Define the count-vector mass on the finite admissible support and cite its normalization lemma.

references.title: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §3.4
Gero Walter, A Technical Note on the Dirichlet-Multinomial Model, 2013

items.title: Dirichlet distribution, including the one-category case
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. For $k\ge2$ and $\alpha_j>0$, the **Dirichlet distribution**
$\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_k)$ is the probability law
on the open probability simplex with density
$$\frac{\Gamma(\alpha_+)}{\prod_j\Gamma(\alpha_j)}
\prod_jp_j^{\alpha_j-1}$$
relative to $dp_1\cdots dp_{k-1}$, with $p_k=1-\sum_{j<k}p_j$. Its
normalization is [[thm-dirichlet-density-normalization]]. For $k=1$, define
the law to be the point mass at $p_1=1$. All coordinates of the parameter
vector must be strictly positive.
items.strategy: Define the proper Dirichlet law using the proved simplex normalization; include the deterministic k=1 case.

references.title: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §3.4
Gero Walter, A Technical Note on the Dirichlet-Multinomial Model, 2013

items.title: Beta-Binomial conjugate update
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $P\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)$ with $\alpha,\beta>0$, and,
conditional on $P=p$, let $Y$ have the Binomial$(n,p)$ law for
$n\in\mathbb N_0$. The data space $\{0,\ldots,n\}$ is equipped with finite
counting measure. For every observed $y\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$, the evidence is
$$m(y)=\binom ny\frac{B(\alpha+y,\beta+n-y)}{B(\alpha,\beta)}
\in(0,\infty),$$
and the posterior is $\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha+y,\beta+n-y)$. The endpoints
$y=0$ and $y=n$ are included; all posterior shape parameters remain positive.
items.strategy: Multiply the normalized Beta prior and Binomial likelihood; integrate the updated kernel and normalize only at finite-positive evidence, including endpoints.

references.title: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §2.1
Johnson, Ott & Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, Chapter 3, §3.1

items.title: Exposure-adjusted Gamma-Poisson conjugate update
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\in\mathbb N_0$, $a,b>0$, and
$\lambda\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(a,b)$ in shape-rate convention. Conditional
on $\lambda$, let $Y_1,\ldots,Y_n$ be independent with
$Y_i\sim\operatorname{Pois}(e_i\lambda)$ for $i=1,\ldots,n$, where each fixed
exposure $e_i\ge0$.
The data space $\mathbb N_0^n$ has counting measure. If some $e_i=0$ but
$y_i>0$, the likelihood and evidence are zero and no posterior quotient is
defined. Otherwise put $E=\sum_i e_i$, $S=\sum_i y_i$, and
$$c(\mathbf e,\mathbf y)=\prod_{i:e_i>0}\frac{e_i^{y_i}}{y_i!},$$
with the empty product one. Then
$$m(\mathbf y)=c(\mathbf e,\mathbf y)\,
\frac{b^a\Gamma(a+S)}{\Gamma(a)(b+E)^{a+S}}\in(0,\infty),$$
and the posterior is $\operatorname{Gamma}(a+S,b+E)$. This includes all-zero
exposures with zero counts, for which the posterior equals the prior.
items.strategy: Separate impossible zero-exposure data, multiply likelihood and prior kernels, and use the Gamma integral with total count and exposure.

references.title: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §§2.1, 2.4
Johnson, Ott & Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, Chapter 5, §5.2.2

items.title: Conjugate update for an exponential-family likelihood
items.statement:
Let $\eta:\Theta\to\Omega$ be measurable, let $n\ge1$, and let $\mu$ be a
sigma-finite data measure. Suppose, given $\theta$, the observations
$Y_1,\ldots,Y_n$ are IID with density
$h(y)\exp\{\eta(\theta)^TT(y)-A(\eta(\theta))\}$ relative to $\mu$. On the
product data space with measure $\mu^{\otimes n}$, assume the resulting joint
density is specified and jointly measurable and that the sampling family is a
parameter-measurable probability kernel. Let the prior be $\Pi_{\chi,\kappa}$ from
[[def-exponential-conjugate-prior-family]] with
$0<Z(\chi,\kappa)<\infty$. For an observed $y_{1:n}$, put
$s=\sum_iT(y_i)$. If $h(y_i)>0$ for each $i$ and
$0<Z(\chi+s,\kappa+n)<\infty$, then the evidence is
$$m(y_{1:n})=\left(\prod_{i=1}^nh(y_i)\right)
\frac{Z(\chi+s,\kappa+n)}{Z(\chi,\kappa)}\in(0,\infty),$$
and the posterior density relative to the parameter measure is
$$\frac{\exp\{\eta(\theta)^T(\chi+s)-(\kappa+n)A(\eta(\theta))\}}
{Z(\chi+s,\kappa+n)}.$$
Thus the update adds $\sum_iT(y_i)$ to $\chi$ and $n$ to $\kappa$ only on
finite-positive evidence fibers.
items.strategy: Multiply the IID exponential-family likelihood and conjugate-form prior; calculate evidence and posterior only on finite-positive evidence fibers.

references.title: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §2.4
Charles J. Geyer, Stat 5421 Lecture Notes: Exponential Families, 2020

items.title: Dirichlet-Multinomial conjugate update
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $p\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1,\ldots,
\alpha_k)$, with each $\alpha_j>0$. Conditional on $p$, observe a
Multinomial$(n,p)$ count vector $y\in\mathbb N_0^k$ with $\sum_jy_j=n$.
For $k\ge2$, the data space is equipped with counting measure on its finite
set of admissible counts. The evidence is
$$m(y)=\frac{n!}{\prod_jy_j!}
\frac{\Gamma(\alpha_+)}{\prod_j\Gamma(\alpha_j)}
\frac{\prod_j\Gamma(\alpha_j+y_j)}{\Gamma(\alpha_++n)}
\in(0,\infty),$$
where $\alpha_+=\sum_j\alpha_j$, and the posterior is
$\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1+y_1,\ldots,\alpha_k+y_k)$.
For $k=1$, the parameter and count are both deterministic and the posterior
equals the prior point mass.
items.strategy: Separate k=1, multiply the Dirichlet and Multinomial kernels, apply simplex normalization, then normalize the posterior.

references.title: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §3.4
Gero Walter, A Technical Note on the Dirichlet-Multinomial Model, 2013

items.title: A positive-variance normal law has its location-scale density
items.statement: Assume AC. For m in R and sigma>0, N(m,sigma^2), defined as the affine pushforward of N(0,1), has Lebesgue density g(m,sigma;y)=(2 pi sigma^2)^(-1/2) exp(-(y-m)^2/(2 sigma^2)).
items.strategy: direct
items.axiom_use: AC is used for the library standard-normal law and implies Countable Choice, which is the hypothesis of the cited C^1 change-of-variables theorem. No further choice is used.

references.title: Andrew Gelman, John B. Carlin, Hal S. Stern, David B. Dunson, Aki Vehtari, and Donald B. Rubin, Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §5.4
Alicia A. Johnson, Miles Q. Ott, and Mine Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, Chapter 16, §16.3

items.title: Known-variance Normal-Normal conjugate update
items.statement:
Assume AC. Let $\mu\sim N(\mu_0,\tau_0^2)$ with $\tau_0^2>0$, and, conditional
on $\mu$, let $Y_1,\ldots,Y_n$ be IID $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ with known
$\sigma^2>0$ and $n\ge1$. The sampling data use the Borel sigma-algebra on
$\mathbb R^n$ with $n$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. For every
$y_{1:n}\in\mathbb R^n$, define
$$V_n=(\tau_0^{-2}+n\sigma^{-2})^{-1},\qquad \mu_n=V_n\left(\frac{\mu_0}{\tau_0^2} +\frac{n\bar y}{\sigma^2}\right),\qquad \bar y=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^ny_i.$$
The evidence is finite and positive, and the posterior is $N(\mu_n,V_n)$.
items.strategy: Multiply the Gaussian prior and IID likelihood, complete the square, evaluate evidence, and identify posterior parameters.

references.title: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §2.5
Johnson, Ott & Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, Chapter 5, §§5.3.1–5.3.4

title: Conjugate families and Gaussian conditioning — Examples

items.title: Gaussian conditioning with singular state covariance
items.statement:
Assume AC. Let $Z=(Z_1,Z_2)\sim N_2(0,I_2)$, where $I_2$ is the $2\times2$
identity matrix, and set $X=(Z_1,Z_1)$ and $Y=Z_1+Z_2$. The state covariance
is singular, $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=2>0$, and the conditional law at every
$y\in\mathbb R$ is
$$X\mid Y=y\sim N_2\left((y/2,y/2),\begin{pmatrix}1/2&1/2\\1/2&1/2\end{pmatrix}\right).$$
items.strategy: Construct a jointly Gaussian state/observation pair with singular state covariance and SPD observed covariance, then apply the conditioner.

references.title: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §3.5 and Appendix A
Simo Särkkä, Bayesian Filtering and Smoothing, Appendix A.1, Lemma A.2

items.title: A Beta(2,3) prior updated by five Bernoulli trials
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. With prior $P\sim\operatorname{Beta}(2,3)$ and $n=5$ Binomial trials, an
observed success count $y=3$ has evidence $4/21$ and posterior
$\operatorname{Beta}(5,5)$. The boundary counts $y=0$ and $y=5$ give proper
posteriors $\operatorname{Beta}(2,8)$ and $\operatorname{Beta}(7,3)$.
items.strategy: Substitute a concrete prior and count into the update formulas; calculate endpoint posteriors.

references.title: Johnson, Ott & Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, Chapter 3, §3.1
Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §2.1

items.title: Gamma-Poisson updating with a zero exposure
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Take $\lambda\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(2,1)$ and two independent counts with
exposures $(e_1,e_2)=(2,0)$. For observed counts $(y_1,y_2)=(3,0)$, the
evidence is $32/243$ and the posterior is $\operatorname{Gamma}(5,3)$. If the
zero-exposure count were instead $y_2=1$, its evidence would be zero and no
posterior quotient would be defined.
items.strategy: Substitute one positive and one zero exposure into the update and verify an impossible zero-exposure count.

references.title: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §2.4
Johnson, Ott & Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, Chapter 5, §5.2.2

items.title: Normal precision pooling with two observations
items.statement:
Assume AC. Let the prior be $\mu\sim N(0,4)$, and, conditionally on $\mu$,
observe independent $Y_1,Y_2\sim N(\mu,1)$. For data $(y_1,y_2)=(1,3)$, the
evidence is finite and positive and the posterior is $N(16/9,4/9)$.
items.strategy: Compute pooled precision and posterior mean for two observations under a proper Gaussian prior.

references.title: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §2.5
Johnson, Ott & Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, Chapter 5, §5.3

items.title: A three-category Dirichlet-Multinomial update
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. With prior $p\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(1,2,1)$,
sample size $n=3$, and observed counts $y=(2,1,0)$, the evidence is $1/10$ and
the posterior is $\operatorname{Dirichlet}(3,3,1)$.
items.strategy: Evaluate one three-category evidence ratio and record its updated Dirichlet vector.

references.title: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §3.4
Gero Walter, A Technical Note on the Dirichlet-Multinomial Model, 2013
